docs.summary: Generate normals if the mesh doesn't have them.
Use smooth (angle-weighted vertex) normals instead of flat/faceted.

Edges sharper than this stay hard when generating smooth normals; the vertices along them are split so each side keeps its own normal. Only used when [`GenerateSmoothNormals`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.AssetImporting.ModelImporterSettings~GenerateSmoothNormals) is on.
Force recalculate normals even if the mesh already has them.
Generate tangent vectors for normal mapping.
Uniform scale applied to all vertex positions.
Build the materials the file describes. Off makes every renderer fall back to the default
Build the animation clips the file describes, and the component that plays them.
Keep morph targets. Off drops them, which is worth doing for a model whose shapes the game never drives: the deltas are a full extra copy of the vertex data per shape.
Merge sibling meshes that share a material into one. Reduces draw calls for models authored as many small parts, at the cost of the parts no longer being separately addressable.
Collapse pass-through nodes, folding their transforms into their children. Sockets, markers, bones, animated nodes and anything carrying metadata are kept regardless.
Node names [`OptimizeHierarchy`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.AssetImporting.ModelImporterSettings~OptimizeHierarchy) must never collapse.
Fail the import when the file fails cross-reference validation, instead of warning and importing whatever survived.
Which scene to import from a file defining several, or -1 for the one the file nominates.

Create a [`Camera`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.Camera) for every camera the file defines. Imported cameras are added disabled, since they describe viewpoints the author set up rather than the one the game renders from.
Create a light component for every punctual light the file defines.

Whether imported clips loop. Model formats carry no looping flag of their own, so this is a choice the importer has to make rather than read. Looping suits the cycles most character animation ships as; a one-shot clip (a door, a chest, an emote) does not.
How the rig is built. Generic drives the bones as the file names them; Humanoid also maps them to the human body, so clips retarget onto any humanoid rig whatever its proportions.
Frames per second clips are sampled at. Curves are resampled on import because a shipped game only ever samples, and frames compress and blend where curves do neither.
Generate a lightmap UV set (UV2) for every mesh via Prowl.Unwrapper. Off by default (it's slow and some models ship their own UV2); the built-in default models force it on.
Per clip overrides, keyed by the name the clip has in the file. A clip with no entry takes the settings above.
Where a material comes from. Null builds every material the file describes; an implementation can point a slot at an asset that was extracted out of the model instead.
Humanoid bone name to the skeleton bone playing it, applied over whatever the auto mapper found. An empty value clears a bone the auto mapper got wrong. Only read for a humanoid rig.

Strategy for turning a model's texture references into textures. Null (the default) uses [`DefaultModelTextureResolver`](#api~Prowl.Runtime.AssetImporting.DefaultModelTextureResolver), which decodes/GPU-uploads immediately - correct for a direct runtime load with no separate asset-tracking step. The editor importer supplies its own resolver that only ever produces database textures, with no decode of its own.
